newsitem.title: BRAZIL: SOCCER-HAVELANGE SAYS THERE IS TOO MUCH FOOTBALL.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-HAVELANGE SAYS THERE IS TOO MUCH FOOTBALL.

text.p: Joao Havelange acknowledged on Tuesday there was too much professional soccer being played in the world but the FIFA boss said his organisation could do little about it.
"I agree that there is an excess of games," said Havelange, who became president of soccer's governing body in 1974 and reconfirmed that he will retire when his mandate expires in 1998.
But he added: "Everyone -- players, directors, doctors, coaching staff -- wants to make money and for that to happen, they have to play."
Havelange said that there was little FIFA could do to remedy the problem as it had no control over fixture lists drawn up by national and continental federations.
Speaking to foreign media based in Brazil, Havelange spent the best part of a 90-minute conference paying a glowing tribute to his own administration.
"When I came to power, FIFA organised only two competitions every four years, the World Cup and the Olympic football tournament," he said. "Today, we have 11 competitions every four years."

"At the 1974 World Cup, the teams had to pay their own flights, accommodation, living expenses and local transport. Today, FIFA pays all this for the competing nations and also gives each team $1 million per game."
He said that during his time, the sport had become a major industry. "General Motors makes $170 billion a year. In the same period, football moves $250 billion. I think I have reached my limit."

Havelange, 80, also took credit for the way the game has taken off in Africa. "When I arrived at FIFA, African football didn't exist. Today, there are not dozens but hundreds of Africans playing in Europe."
"Africa has the athletic ability but they need more organisation. You need backup to put a team on the field."
Of his decision to retire, Havelange, who remained neutral on any potential replacements, said: "It's easy in life to start something. It's much more difficult to decide the right moment to stop."
